questions.enonce_markdown:
The Group VII elements of the Periodic Table are called Halogens.

(i) List these elements in order of increasing atomic number indicating their physical states.

(ii) What accounts for the variation in the physical states of the Halogens? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** In order of increasing atomic number, with the state at room temperature and pressure:

| Element | Formula | Physical state at r.t.p. |
|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | $\mathrm{F_2}$ | gas (pale yellow) |
| Chlorine | $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ | gas (greenish-yellow) |
| Bromine | $\mathrm{Br_2}$ | volatile liquid (red-brown) |
| Iodine | $\mathrm{I_2}$ | solid (grey-black, gives a violet vapour on warming) |
| Astatine | $\mathrm{At_2}$ | solid (radioactive, very rare) |

**(ii)** The halogens are **simple molecular substances made of diatomic molecules**. The molecules are held together in the solid and liquid states by weak **intermolecular van der Waals (London dispersion) forces**, not by the strong covalent bond inside the molecule (which is not broken on melting or boiling). The strength of the London forces **increases down the group as the molecules get bigger, with more electrons, so more polarisable** ($M_r$: 38, 71, 160, 254). More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the melting and boiling points increase and the state changes from gas ($\mathrm{F_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$) to liquid ($\mathrm{Br_2}$) to solid ($\mathrm{I_2}$, $\mathrm{At_2}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Explain why hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide cannot be prepared conveniently by reacting their corresponding potassium salts with concentrated sulphuric acid

(iii) Write a balanced chemical equation showing how hydrogen bromide can be prepared in the laboratory. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Concentrated sulphuric acid first displaces the hydrogen halide, e.g. $\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{KHSO_4} + \mathrm{HBr}$. But concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ is also an **oxidising agent**, and **HBr and HI are good reducing agents** (the halide ions $\mathrm{Br^-}$ and $\mathrm{I^-}$ are easily oxidised, the more so the larger the ion). The hydrogen halide is therefore **oxidised to the halogen** as soon as it forms, and the products are contaminated:

- $2\mathrm{HBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$ (red-brown bromine vapour)
- $8\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{I_2} + \mathrm{H_2S} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$ (violet iodine vapour, smell of bad eggs; iodide reduces the acid further than bromide does)

Only a poor yield of pure HBr or HI is obtained. (HCl is not oxidised by concentrated sulphuric acid, so chloride salts work.)

**(iii)** Use a **non-oxidising acid**: heat a bromide with concentrated **phosphoric(V) acid**:

$\mathrm{KBr(s)} + \mathrm{H_3PO_4(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{KH_2PO_4(s)} + \mathrm{HBr(g)}$

(Alternative: add water to phosphorus tribromide, made in situ from red phosphorus and bromine: $\mathrm{PBr_3} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_3PO_3} + 3\mathrm{HBr}$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Most toothpastes are fluorinated and kitchen salt is iodinated. State the importance of

(i) fluorinating tooth paste

(ii) iodinating kitchen salt
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Fluorinating toothpaste.** Fluoride ions **strengthen the tooth enamel**: they replace hydroxide ions in the enamel (hydroxyapatite, $\mathrm{Ca_5(PO_4)_3OH}$) to form **fluoroapatite**, $\mathrm{Ca_5(PO_4)_3F}$, which is harder and **more resistant to attack by the acids** made by bacteria from sugars, so it **prevents tooth decay (dental caries)**.

**(ii) Iodinating kitchen salt.** Iodine is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone **thyroxine**. An iodine-deficient diet causes **goitre** (swelling of the thyroid gland) and in children poor physical and mental development (cretinism). Adding a small amount of iodide or iodate to table salt, which everybody eats, **prevents these iodine-deficiency disorders**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements of Group I and II elements of the Periodic Table are called S-block elements,

(i) Write the valence electronic configurations of the Groups I and II elements

(ii) How do the reactions of the Group II elements with water vary down the group? Explain the trend.

(iii) Write balanced chemical equations to show the reactions of the following elements with cold water.

$\mathrm{Na(s)}$:

$\mathrm{Mg(s)}$:

(iv) Arrange the hydroxides of Group II elements (Be to Ba) in decreasing order of solubility beginning with the most soluble. Explain the trend.

(v) State two ways in which the chemistry of lithium or its compounds differ from those of other alkali elements. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The outer electrons occupy an s sub-shell ($n$ is the period number):

- **Group I:** $ns^1$ (e.g. Na: $3s^1$)
- **Group II:** $ns^2$ (e.g. Mg: $3s^2$)

**(ii) Trend.** The reaction with water becomes **more vigorous down the group**: beryllium does not react (even with steam); magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water (a few bubbles), but burns in steam to give $\mathrm{MgO}$ and $\mathrm{H_2}$; calcium reacts steadily with cold water, giving bubbles of hydrogen and a milky suspension of $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$; strontium and barium react more and more vigorously. General equation: $\mathrm{M(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{M(OH)_2} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$.

**Explanation:** each atom has to lose its two outer electrons. Down the group the atomic radius increases and there is more shielding by inner shells, so the outer electrons are held less strongly: the **ionisation energy falls**, the metal loses electrons more easily and is a stronger reducing agent ($E^{\circ}$ becomes more negative: $\mathrm{Mg}$ $-2.37\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Ca}$ $-2.87\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Ba}$ $-2.91\ \mathrm{V}$). Reactivity increases.

**(iii)**

- $2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$ (vigorous, the sodium melts and darts about)
- $\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg(OH)_2(s)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$ (very slow with cold water; $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ is only slightly soluble)

**(iv) Solubility of the hydroxides** (decreasing, most soluble first):

$\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2} > \mathrm{Sr(OH)_2} > \mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} > \mathrm{Mg(OH)_2} > \mathrm{Be(OH)_2}$

**Explanation:** dissolving requires the lattice enthalpy to be overcome by the hydration enthalpies of the ions. The hydroxide ion is small, so the lattice enthalpy depends strongly on the size of the cation and falls steeply as the cation gets bigger; the hydration enthalpy of the $\mathrm{M^{2+}}$ ion also falls down the group, but **less steeply than the lattice enthalpy**. The enthalpy of solution therefore becomes more favourable (less endothermic) down the group and the solubility **increases**. ($\mathrm{Be(OH)_2}$ is practically insoluble in water; it is amphoteric and dissolves in excess alkali.)

**(v) Lithium differs from the other alkali metals** (it resembles magnesium, a **diagonal relationship**). Any two of:

- On burning in air lithium forms the **normal oxide $\mathrm{Li_2O}$** ($4\mathrm{Li} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_2O}$), whereas sodium forms the peroxide $\mathrm{Na_2O_2}$ and the others superoxides.
- It **reacts with nitrogen** to form the nitride, $6\mathrm{Li} + \mathrm{N_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_3N}$; the other alkali metals do not.
- Its **carbonate and nitrate decompose on heating** to the oxide ($\mathrm{Li_2CO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$; $4\mathrm{LiNO_3} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li_2O} + 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$), while the carbonates of the other alkali metals are stable to heat and their nitrates give the nitrite and oxygen.
- Its **hydroxide, carbonate and fluoride are much less soluble** than those of the other alkali metals, and its compounds show more covalent character; lithium also reacts more slowly with water.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Nitric acid is manufactured by the catalytic oxidation of ammonia.

(i) Write a balanced equation giving the reaction conditions for the conversion of ammonia to nitrogen monoxide

(ii) Give the formula and name of a compound of nitrogen in the +5 oxidation state commonly used as a fertilizer *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Ostwald process, first stage: ammonia and excess air (oxygen) are passed over a **platinum-rhodium gauze catalyst** at about **800-900 $^\circ$C** (about 1100 K) and a pressure of **1 to 10 atm**:

$4\mathrm{NH_3(g)} + 5\mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Pt/Rh},\ 800\text{-}900\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\ } 4\mathrm{NO(g)} + 6\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$

(Atom check: N 4 = 4; H 12 = 12; O 10 = 4 + 6.) The reaction is exothermic, so the gauze stays hot without extra heating; NO is then oxidised to $\mathrm{NO_2}$, which is absorbed in water in the presence of air to give $\mathrm{HNO_3}$.

**(ii)** **Ammonium nitrate, $\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}$**, the most widely used nitrogen fertilizer; its nitrate ion contains nitrogen in the +5 oxidation state (the nitrogen in $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ is $-3$). Other nitrates of nitrogen in the +5 state used as fertilizers: potassium nitrate $\mathrm{KNO_3}$, sodium nitrate $\mathrm{NaNO_3}$, calcium nitrate $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$.
